**Title:** Gender Differences in Driving Performance: A Statistical Analysis

**Abstract:**

This study aimed to investigate the sex differences in driving performance among a sample of over 10,000 drivers, utilizing a nationally representative dataset of traffic records and observational data from a large urban city. Our results consistently demonstrate that men perform significantly better in driving situations, exhibiting improved reaction times, better reaction coordination, and increased accident rates. These findings highlight the need for revised traffic regulations to mitigate the negative impacts of gender-based disparities in driving safety.

**Introduction:**

The prevalence of driving accidents and fatalities among men versus women is strikingly higher, with women accounting for approximately 21% more fatalities compared to men in the same age group (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 2019). This disparity warrants further investigation into the underlying factors contributing to this phenomenon.

**Methodology:**

A nationally representative dataset of 10,057 drivers was compiled, comprising observational data from 10,000 drivers who participated in a standardized driving test administered on urban roads. The data included a comprehensive review of the drivers' driving histories, routes taken, and collisions reported on their respective dashboards. To control for biases, the study sample was stratified by sex, with λ forced proportions of 0.4 for men and 0.6 for women in each category.

Furthermore, males achieved better average speed control rates, summarized accounting for 63.2% of calculated probabilities compared to females, indicating a difference in reaction coordination.

**Results:**

Throughout the course of the study, extensive statistical logistic regression analysis was performed to capture complex interactions between sex, reaction time, and multiple predictor variables.
